headline: Arizona gets America's newest national park

sources.title: Chiricahua's towering spires now stand as Arizona's newest national park (AP via AZFamily)
Chiricahua National Monument officially named country's newest national park (13 News KOLD)
This 'hidden gem' in Arizona just became America's newest national park (Deseret News)
Chiricahua National Park (U.S. National Park Service)

chunks.text: America has a new national park, full of tall, unusual rocks. On October 20, 2026, President Trump signed a law that turned Chiricahua, a [[national monument]] in southern Arizona, into the country's 64th national park. It is the first new national park in six years. The park {{stands out}} for its thousands of stone [[spires]] and [[balanced rocks]]. Early [[settlers]] called it the "Wonderland of Rocks." The land was first {{set aside}} for [[protection]] in 1924.

verbs.why: Her red coat stands out in a crowd. Tall buildings stand out against the evening sky. The park stands out for its thousands of stone spires and balanced rocks.

verbs.correct: To keep land for a special use
verbs.wrong: To build roads across the land
verbs.why: Many cities set aside land for public gardens. Some farmers set aside a field for wild birds. The land was first set aside for protection in 1924.

chunks.text: The rocks formed after a huge [[volcanic eruption]] about 27 million years ago. Over millions of years, wind and water slowly {{wore the rock away}}. This left tall [[columns]] of stone. The area was home to the Chiricahua Apache, a Native American people. Native Americans called it the "Land of Standing-Up Rocks." Making the site a national park took years of work by Arizona [[lawmakers]]. That work {{paid off}} when Congress passed the bill in late September with [[support from both parties]].

verbs.correct: To slowly remove bits of rock
verbs.wrong: To slowly turn rock into glass
verbs.why: Rivers wear away stone over a very long time. Ocean waves wear away the cliffs a little each year. Over millions of years, wind and water slowly wore the rock away.

verbs.correct: To bring success after hard work
verbs.wrong: To need a second vote in Congress
verbs.why: Hard study pays off at exam time. Saving a little money each month pays off later. That work paid off when Congress passed the bill in late September with support from both parties.

chunks.text: Visitors have [[plenty]] to see and do. An eight-mile [[scenic drive]] winds past rock towers to a high [[viewpoint]]. From there, people {{take in}} [[wide views]] of the standing rocks. Hikers can {{head out}} on 17 miles of [[trails]], from easy walks to hard climbs. Visitors can also {{check out}} an old [[guest ranch]] or camp under [[dark night skies]].

verbs.correct: To see and enjoy a view
verbs.wrong: To draw a picture of something
verbs.why: We sit on the hill and take in the sunset. Tourists take in the city from the top of the tower. From there, people take in wide views of the standing rocks.

verbs.wrong: To sign a list at the gate
verbs.why: We head out early when the weather is hot. Many families head out to the beach on Saturdays. Hikers can head out on 17 miles of trails, from easy walks to hard climbs.

verbs.correct: To visit and see a place
verbs.why: Tourists check out the old church in the town square. My friends check out every new cafe in town. Visitors can also check out an old guest ranch or camp under dark night skies.

chunks.text: About 70,000 people visited the site in 2025. The interior secretary, whose department runs the national parks, expects that number to {{go up}} a lot. He {{pointed out}} that [[budgets]] for trails, water systems and [[visitor centers]] get bigger when a site becomes a national park. Leaders in a small town of 3,500 people nearby hope the park will {{bring in}} more [[tourists]]. The secretary said the first job is to {{put up}} signs with the park's new name.

verbs.why: Gas prices go up in the summer. Rents go up when a city grows fast. The interior secretary, whose department runs the national parks, expects that number to go up a lot.

verbs.why: My friend always points out that the bus is cheaper. Good teachers point out the most common mistakes. He pointed out that budgets for trails, water systems and visitor centers get bigger when a site becomes a national park.

verbs.wrong: To let people camp for free
verbs.why: A good festival brings in visitors from far away. Free concerts bring in big crowds. Leaders in a small town of 3,500 people nearby hope the park will bring in more tourists.

verbs.wrong: To print the new name on maps
verbs.why: Stores put up signs for their big sales. Neighbors put up posters when a pet is lost. The secretary said the first job is to put up signs with the park's new name.

mainIdea.s: A rocky area in southern Arizona has become the country's newest national park after years of work by lawmakers. Officials and local leaders expect it to draw more visitors.
mainIdea.why: Chiricahua became the 64th national park in October 2026. Officials expect visitor numbers to go up, and a nearby town hopes for more tourists.

mainIdea.s: A protected rock area in Arizona was made a national park because too many people were visiting it. Officials now plan to limit how many hikers can enter the park each day.
mainIdea.why: Close, but officials want more visitors, not fewer. The interior secretary expects visitor numbers to go up, and a nearby town hopes the park will bring in tourists.

mainIdea.s: Heavy rain has closed several hiking trails in a national park in northern Arizona. Rangers say the paths will stay shut until crews repair the storm damage next spring.
mainIdea.why: This news is about a new national park in southern Arizona. It stands out for its tall stone spires and balanced rocks.

lines.text: Did you hear that Arizona has a new national park?
Really? I thought Arizona already had the Grand Canyon.
It does. This one is called Chiricahua. It's in the south, and it's the first new national park in six years.
It {{stands out}} for its rocks. There are thousands of tall stone towers and balanced rocks.
How did they get like that?
Wind and water {{wore the rock away}} over millions of years.
Wow. Was the land protected before?
Yes, it was {{set aside}} in 1924. Now it finally has the bigger title.
So what can you do there?
You can {{take in}} the views from a high viewpoint, or {{head out}} on the trails.
The photos look [[out of this world]]. It sounds like a real [[hidden gem]].
It is. It's a bit [[off the beaten path]], far from the big cities.
A small one. Leaders there hope the park will {{bring in}} more tourists, and officials expect visitor numbers to {{go up}}.
That makes sense. Life [[in the middle of nowhere]] can be hard for a small town.
Fun fact: early settlers called it the Wonderland of Rocks.
I'd love to {{check out}} those rocks someday. I'm adding it to my [[bucket list]].
